Our toolchain doesn't support C++ language but our project type is
proposed in the "New project" wizard when the end-user selects "Managed Make C++ Projects". So, it may be confusing for our end-users that select a C++ projects but can't build it. It could be nice to have available, only wizards supported by the tool.

Is it possible to have a way to do it in next CDT version ? Can a filtering be done in the wizards ?

Regards,
Jerome

Filtering is available in extensions of the CDT wizards. See CDTMainWizardPage.filterItems().

CNewWizards can also selectively filter EntryDescriptors in their createItems() method by just not creating any items that are not appliccable.

However, we need a way to hide some things from the generic CDT wizard. We also have this problem in that remote toolchains from RDT will show up in the regular CDT project wizard, and they won't work on local projects.

toolchains already allow you to specify an isToolchainSupported attribute that provides a Java callback to determine whether the given toolchain is shown by default. This interface does not provide any context however about which wizard is being displayed.

I suggest that we need to be able to:
- provide a callback for toolchains that has more context information
- provide callbacks with similar granularity for project types

Well the issue here is that the default content type extensions are locked. So, even if you create a new mapping for .c, you haven't removed the old one.

Not really sure what to do about this, if anything.

That may be a bad default for CDT, but is a perfectly reasonable default for other language tools. We won't be changing the default at the platform level. However, there are many options available for changing this default. Products can alter this in their plugin_customization.ini, and there is API to change this programmatically (IWorkspaceDescription.setAutoBuilding(...)). One option is to prompt the user when the first CDT project is created to ask if they want to turn off autobuild, or incorporate that option into the CDT project wizard. 

Finally, the CDT builder itself can be configured to not respond to auto-build events. I added this support specifically for CDT early last year, so it's disappointing that it has not been adopted (see bug 60803). Moving back to CDT for consideration of these options.

The .cdtbuild file of the sample project contains the "hidden" flag set. If you remove that flag, everything will work fine.

The root cause of the issue is that the Managed Build Info gets accessed before the project tree gets loadded into the workspace.
E.g. the workspace refresh that is performed after the project import is performed after the project build request is performed (when autobuild is on).
As a result the .cdtbuild file is not seen at that time.
The .cdtbuild file load is performed using standard java File API, while the file store (initiated by the project update mechanism in the sample project) is performed via eclipse IResource API.
The Managed Build Info serialization logic examines whether the .cdtbuild file exists in the workspace and if not, tries to create the one using the IFile.create(). The method fails in case the underlying resource exists and is "hidden".

Sometime ago I raised a bug against the platform regarding the project-scoped preferences inaccessibility from OPEN event handler on project import (see bug# 139911). The root cause of that problem was the same as the one for this bug.
The bug was closed as WONTFIX.

I'm not sure whether invoking build before importing(refreshing) the complete project tree stands within eclipse build ideology. I'm going to raise a bug againts platform to get more clarification on this.

The quick solution for this bug for now could be to use java File API for storing the build info.

Adding a pipe > logfile.txt proves this.

I've searched and I can't find the problem mentioned anywhere on the web, so firstly, I need somebody to just confirm that I'm not being stupid somewhere.

Solved the problem!!!

Not a problem with CDT, it was a problem with make.exe

My machine had two copies of make.exe, one earier in the path than the other. It was picking the wrong one for the build, not the one from the cross arm toolchain folder - perhaps there should be some control over which make is being used?

Anyway, the make being used was somehow munging the path when running external commands, thus it could not find

ne for the build, not the one from the cross arm toolchain folder - perhaps there should be some control over which make is being used?

Anyway, the make being used was somehow munging the path when running external commands, thus it could not find subwcrev.exe.

Copying subwcrev.exe to the project folder compouned the problem. Subwcrev could not find its .dll, it normally reports this using a dialogue box, but somehow eclipse was supressing this dialogue.

I solved the problem using a dummy make file that just called the pre.bat, this allowed the dialogue to appear indicating the source of the problem.


Conclusion:
I would not consider this bug fixed, there are two possible areas for improvement.
1: Prevent eclipse from supressing dialogue boxes
2: Allow a means to control which make.exe the build uses, just as we can control which gcc or as is used.

1. foo.c:
#include "foo.h"
int main () {return 0;}

2. foo.h:
#ifndef _FOO_H_
#define _FOO_H_

#endif

Assume that our project already was built. Now insert in foo.h following string:
#include "missing.h"

Note: file missing.h doesn't exist.

When foo.h is saved foo.c would be recompiled (that's correct). Now we have project with an error. Then fix the error: just remove '#include "missing.h"' from foo.h and save it. Well, foo.c IS NOT recompiled because foo.d is empty now and foo.o still exists!

I can reproduce this problem for the case there are two files included in the build having same name and different extensions, residing in one folder, e.g. foo.c and foo.cpp. 

This is the old MBS issue, i.e. neither the GNU makefile generator used for the external make builder nor the Internal Builder can handle this case.
More than that the Internal Builder behaves behaves more correct in this case, i.e. it fails, while the GNU makefile generator sielently procedes and can generate wrong/inclomplete binary.

The reason for the issue is that by default it is assumed that the output file for the . file is the . file.
So in in case we have e.g. foo.c and foo.cpp files in one directory the generated file for both of them will be foo.o for the gnu tool-chain.
Now suppose the foo.c is built first and the foo.o is created. After that foo.cpp is built. the foo.o gets overwritten.
The resulting binary will include include only foo.o created from the foo.cpp

There is no easy way to add compilation options to all new created projects. For example, adding "-Wextra" to every newly created C/C++ managed make project. The "Managed Build System Extensibility Document" describes a way for defining a new project type, but most likely that is out of proportion for the "-Wextra" example.

Searching the bug database I could not find a similar bug report, but I can hardly believe that no one have considered this before.

I guess this should be possible in CDT 4.0. What you might want to do is:

1. register the ICProjectDescriptionListener with the CCoreModel.addCProjectDescriptionListener() to handle the CProjectDescriptionEvent.ABOUT_TO_APPLY event.

2. In your event handler you would need to obtain the ICDescriptionDelta via 
CProjectDescriptionEvent.getProjectDelta()

3. the delta.getDeltaKind() should be ICDescriptionDelta.ADDED for the newly created projects

4. ICProjectDescription newDes = (ICProjectDescription)delta.getNewSetting();

ICConfiguration cfgDess[] = newDes.getConfigurations()

foreach cfgDess do
 IConfiguration cfg = ManagedBuildManager.getConfigurationForDescription(cfgDes);
 ..get the tools/options needed and perform adjustments..
end do

Hope the above works.. Does this suite your needs?

Mikhail

with

CDT 6.0 (CDT_6_0 tag). When the file(s) is excluded from build (or included after being excluded), then instead of rebuilding a whole project (can be hundreds of files), only the linker is called to create an artifact. The implementation changes the artifact modification time prior to one of the sources, thus making it outdated. Tested with internal and external builders.

Created attachment 167339
Updated patch

The previous patch just touched the artifact, to force the output tool (e.g. linker) to regenerate it. It didn't take into account that the project may include: file.S and file.c, where one of them is active and another is excluded. Switching between these files with include/exclude, should recompile the source. This patch touches the excluded object, to make sure it is compiled when a file with the same base name is included.
Based on CDT_6_0_0 tag.

To recouple the previous comments:
-) When the source file is excluded from build, then at the next build, the project is cleaned before build, causing a full build instead of just calling the linker.
-) When a source file is included back, the same behavior repeats. Instead, it should only build the included source if needed and link.
-) CDT should support excluding of file.c and then including file.S, both having the same output extension. It should only build file.S, even when file.o is newer and then call linker.

Ideally, the MBS (Configuration class?) should track the delta between the builds. If a source was excluded, it should add its output and artifact to the list of "changed" resources. During the build, it should either delete these outputs or change their modification time to trigger their build.

There were no comments for a long time and unfortunately in CDT 5.0 it is still not fixed.
Though this may not seem so important for small projects, it becomes very significant for medium/large projects with long compilation times.

I'd like to discuss a solution for this problem. Today, when the user includes or excludes a source file(s), CDT calls the setSourceEntries(ICSourceEntries[]) method through multiple configuration-related classes. Finally, it comes to Configuration.setSourceEntries(ICSourceEntries[]), which in turn calls Configuration.setSourceEntries(ICSourceEntries[], boolean setRebuildState) with setRebuildState=TRUE. This is why the projects are cleaned and rebuilt.
If this last call is modified to Configuration.setSourceEntries(ICSourceEntries[], FALSE), then the following happens. If executable exists and the user runs exclude/include wizard and no source was modified, then attempting to build a project does nothing, because make/internal builder find the executable up-to-date. If any of the source files were modified after the last build, then after exclude/include, the executable is built with a modified source(s) and correct set of objects.

Hi Doug,

I guess the root cause of your problem is in "inconsistency" of the "clone" configuration concept used by the option settings UI (and most other CDT project settings UI) and the scanner discovery settings mechanism that (historically) knows nothing about the "clone" configuration concept.

Some background: while project settings modifications all changes are being made to the "clone" configuration which is actually a copy of the "cached" project configuration. 
All UI is communicating directly to this configuration thus ensuring the UI settings integrity, e.g. in case one setting change results in some other settings change, the change will be reflected in UI.
In case of OK the "clone" configuration gets applied.
In case of CANCEL the "clone" configuration gets simply discarded.
In case of APPLY all settings from the "clone" configuration get copied to the other "clone" configuration which then gets applied.

From the option value handler mechanism perspective the "EVENT_APPLY" event is posted when the option value is modified. As a result you are receiving this event when the option value is modified in UI and when the "APPLY" button is pressed since in this case the other "clone" configuration (to be applied) receives all option values from the currently used one. And you see no events on CANCEL because in this case the "clone" gets simply discarded and on OK because in this case the "clone" gets applied with the current modifications being made with no additions option modifications.
 This approach works fine till you are using/adjusting settings within

" as well as from the "real". As a result, e.g. it was inappropriate to access e.g. the ManagedBuildInfo since this might result in a permanent storing of temporary settings.

Bug 348700 fixed a severe regression late in the game. This bug is for following-up with more investigation and probably a cleaner solution.

Particularly, in VT100TerminalControl#disconnectTerminal(),

- The Connector should likely be disconnected BEFORE terminating the reader job
 (otherwise with high data volume, the connector can write into a pipe that's
 no longer being read from, or even closed)

- The Reader should have a more clean method of terminating fast (other than
 interrupting the entire Thread, which may cause InterruptedException at a
 time where it's not desired, for instance while processing characters - 
 see bug 333613 comment 2)

- Revisit whether it makes sense to keep the PipedInputStream alive and 
 open for the entire lifetime of the VT100TerminalControl, even when 
 different connections read/write to it.

Test cases for these improvement include
- disconnect / reconnect terminals
 - both from the Terminal (pressing button)
 - and from the remote side (pull network cable, connection-lost, EOF)
- Terminate Eclipse with multiple terminals open.
Michael Scharf has found a potential race condition with the fix in bug 348700 (see comments there), which we should address immediately after Indigo.

 500 msec. This should be sufficient to allow doing job.join() timely.

 PipedOutputStream, in order to trigger a notify on the pipe to exit
 waitForAvailable().

- my auto-build command should be "make mystub" not "make all"

Generally speaking, all of the Make Builder properties tab of a Standard Make
are subject to a user's personal preferences. Managed Make properties
have similar problems; see bug54202 for a start.

All of these options can be overridden by checking out the appropriate
files (.project), and never checking those personal changes back in.
This approach is error-prone because that same file may also contain
legitimate team-worthy changes to referenced projects, error parsers,
include paths, defined symbols, etc.

Using managed make there is no way to specify the final name of a shared 
library nor the soname in the build properties. 
 
No matter how I configure the build options for a project, the resulting 
auto-generated Makefile insists on naming the resulting library 
file  libFOO.so  forcing me to rename it before I can create the proper 
symlinks manually (while testing) or before ldconfig will do so for me (when 
installing) 
 
When building the library (libFOO in this example), to properly deal with 
different versions of the library I need to set a proper soname on it, and 
name the library properly to let ldconfig create the proper links to the 
latest version of the library. 
So, say this is version 1.2.3 of libFOO, then I need a soname of libFOO.so.1 
and the real library filename would be libFOO.so.1.2.3 then when installing the 
library I (or ldconfig) will create a link from the soname to the library: 
libFOO.so.1 --> libFOO.so.1.2.3 
and then a link for apps to use when linking against -lFOO : 
libFOO.so --> libFOO.so.1 (some setups will use libFOO.so --> libFOO.so.1.2.3) 
 
So, when building I really need the resulting file to be named 
libFOO.so.1.2.3 or I have to do manual renaming before install/use 
But, no matter what I do, Eclipse+CDT insist on naming the library for my 
FOO project libFOO.so  
What is needed is a way to specify the soname for the lib in the build 
preferences, only possible workaround at the moment is to specify 
-Wl,-soname,libFOO.so.1 in the Miscellaneous settings. 
 
The closest I can get is (by specifying most of the stuff in the Misc 
sections) is to get my object files build like this : 
 
g++ -O0 -g3 -Wall -fPIC -c -o a.o a.cpp 
g++ -O0 -g3 -Wall -fPIC -c -o b.o

g++ -O0 -g3 -Wall -fPIC -c -o a.o a.cpp

it's almost perfect. What would make it 100% perfect would be a box

1. Put a Gnu compiler on your path via symlink:

setenv PATH ~/gnulink/bin:$PATH

2. Create a Std Make project. Turn on Automated Path Discovery.
Compile the project.
The project will compile, finding all of its necessary includes and libs.
(The compiler knows where to find its bits.)

3. Examine the paths:
~/gnulink/include is listed as a removed path, since it does not exist.
(Similarly with other paths.)

EXPECTED: ~/gnulink/bin/../include is resolvable and, because of the 
symlink, should not be collapsed into ~/gnulink/include.

(As a clarification, it isn't the tilde which is the problem;
I should have expressed a true path like /home/bnicolle/gnulink/bin.
The problem is the symbolic link on the file-path.)

4. From the command-line, set up:
> mkdir /temp/project /temp/project/src /temp/project/inc
> ln -s /temp/project/src /home/bnicolle/project_src_link
5. Add to your compile line:
-I/home/bnicolle/project_src_link/../inc
6. Rebuild and examine your Discovered Paths
/home/bnicolle/inc
is listed under Removed paths.

In the case of compiler intrinsics (step 3), the Removed path displays:

In the case of Makefile-related paths (step 6), the Removed path displays:
/home/bnicolle/inc

In both cases, Scanner Config collapses the " /../" out of the path.

Make allows you to specify which shell is used to execute the scriptlets it 
uses to perform tasks. By specifying a custom psuedo shell that just takes the 
commands and passes them through to a real shell accurate information about the 
build process can be gleaned, even in instances with -j flags greater than 1. 
 
This method also improves correctness as make does not necessarily echo the 
output of every build operation to stdout (there are mechanisms that are used 
in the wild that suppress such output selectively).
Are you planning to contribute design/code for this enhancement?

If I spend the time to create a large number of make 
targets on a directory, then I need to rename the directory
to something else (or copy it) the make targets should
move/copy with it. Currently when a directory is 
renamed, the make targets just dissappear, but then 
re-appear if I create a new directory using the old
name. 

This is likely not intuitive behaviour and since the set-up
cost of make targets is high, it would help to minimize
frustration.
There is a workaround:
As you might have noticed the make targets are not removed from the .cprojects file (that is why they reappear if you create a new folder with the old name). Thus, you can change the folder name in the .cprojects file manually and have your make targets back. Not very intuitive but it just works.
